paragraphs.heading: Where is God when I suffer
paragraphs.edited: In the midst of our suffering, it's easy to feel alone, to feel isolated. When we see or experience suffering, it's natural to ask a lot of questions. Why am I suffering? Am I alone? Is my suffering going to end? Why is God allowing me to suffer? Where is God when I suffer, and what is Christianity's unique response to suffering and pain? Let me share a story that might help.

paragraphs.heading: Father Damien
paragraphs.edited: In 1873, a priest by the name of Father Damien heard about a colony of lepers who were living and dying without anybody to care for them. So, with full awareness of the risk, Father Damien went and became a priest for this colony of lepers. He prayed for them. He preached to them. He changed their wounds. He built caskets. He buried many of them. For 12 years, with deep compassion and care, he loved this colony of lepers, so they would know and experience the love of God. One Sunday evening, however, everything changed. Father Damien stood before the people with leprosy and he spoke these two words. He said, "We lepers." He opened up his robe and showed the first physical signs of leprosy. Father Damien had become a leper.

paragraphs.edited: Let me ask you a couple of questions about the story. First, how did the view of the lepers change toward Father Damien when he became a leper? No doubt, beforehand they knew that he loved them. They saw his willingness to sacrifice everything for them, but now, when he got leprosy, everything was different. Now he could understand them in a new way. They saw the depth of his sacrifice for them. He could empathize with them in a personal way.

paragraphs.heading: God is right there with us
paragraphs.edited: The second question is, is God's response to our suffering more like Father Damien before he got leprosy, or after? If we stop and we think about the life, ministry and death of Jesus, I think the answer is clear. It's after. See, God didn't just send a prophet or an angel or a book, as important as those are. In the person of Jesus Christ, God came down personally and has experienced our pain. We are not abandoned to our suffering and our pain. So part of the answer to "where is God when I suffer" is that God is right there suffering with us.

paragraphs.heading: A God who has suffered
paragraphs.edited: Think about the symbols for the various world religions. You've got the statue of Buddha for Buddhism, the gate for Shintoism, the crescent and the sword for Islam, or the Star of David for Judaism. Yet for Christianity, the most defining image, the most defining symbol, is the cross: a picture of the creator of the universe stepped down in human flesh, suffering for us. We follow and worship a God who has suffered.

paragraphs.edited: Isaiah the prophet said the coming Messiah would be a man of sorrows, familiar with suffering. And in the book of Hebrews, the author writes in chapter 4 that we do not follow a high priest who's unable to sympathize with us, but we have a high priest who's been tempted and tested in every way like we are. He understands our weaknesses, but is without sin.

For example, if you're in physical pain and you think, gosh, I'm in so much pain, God doesn't understand what I'm going through, remember that Jesus was crucified and experienced excruciating physical pain. If you've gone through relational difficulties, and maybe somebody's betrayed you or left you out, and you think, God, you don't understand, remember that during his lifetime much of Jesus' family didn't believe in him, and in fact he was betrayed by one of his closest disciples. paragraphs.edited: Many times what our suffering enables us to do is to have empathy for other people and build a deeper sense of community. Take the example of Father Damien contracting leprosy. As painful and as hurtful as that is, it enabled him to be in a new community and experience the love of a people that wasn't there before.

paragraphs.heading: Will you trust me?
paragraphs.edited: Ultimately, I might not be able to explain why you, or me, or anyone else experiences a particular kind of suffering. Sometimes we might know in this life, but many times it won't be until we get to eternity. But I know this. I know that God is good. I know that God has not abandoned us in our suffering. I know God is asking you and me the same question he asked Job thousands of years ago, when Job was suffering immensely. He said, Job, will you trust me?

paragraphs.heading: What you meant for evil
paragraphs.edited: It's important to remember that God can take our greatest pain, our greatest suffering, and turn it to good. We see this in the life of Joseph, a story that you know. Joseph is sold into slavery by his own brothers and ends up in prison, but rises up through God's hand to be second in command in Egypt, and is able to save his family from famine. When he finally talks with his brothers and they realize his identity, they're afraid that he might take retribution against them. But what does he say? He essentially says, don't worry. What you meant for evil, God meant for good.

paragraphs.edited: When Jesus was arrested and crucified, his apostles thought that all had been lost. This movement and person they had been following for roughly three years seemingly had come to an end. They were devastated. But what they didn't realize at that moment is that in their darkest hour, God had never let go of the steering wheel. He was still in control and working his greatest good. We see it's through the resurrection that we know that death does not have the end. Suffering is not the end, and this world will ultimately be redeemed.

paragraphs.heading: Death, where is your sting?
paragraphs.edited: Suffering and pain do not have the final word. Jesus is risen. That's right, Jesus is risen. That's why the Apostle Paul, who experienced tremendous suffering, could shout with an air of defiance in 1 Corinthians 15, a chapter on the resurrection: "Death, where's your victory? Death, where's your sting?"
